track.note: No forecasts resolved yet. The first resolve late September (Brent band, Sep 24) into October (Xi summit and the Chinese-bank sanctions question, Oct 1). Every score lands here as it happens — the misses included.

plumbing.read: The buffer is gone and the official gold bid has stopped caring about price. ON RRP sits at $0.17B, the Fed balance sheet is quietly expanding, and central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the very quarter gold suffered its worst fall since 2013. But the milkshake tape — oil AND dollar rising together — is still NOT printing: the broad dollar is soft at 118.1, down 2.4% on the month, and that is the live evidence against escalation. Pressure sits in the plumbing, not yet in the price.
plumbing.epoch: E6 still open — the Sept-2019 repo confession never closed — running alongside E7, the weaponized-settlement rail opened by the 2022 reserve freeze that the record official gold bid is a late chapter of.

easy.bottomLine: America says the Strait of Hormuz is now clear of mines. But the insurance companies that ships depend on have not agreed, and until they do, the oil route stays mostly shut no matter what any government announces.
easy.risk: Still tense, and pulling in two directions at once. The Gulf is slowly getting better - there is a mine-free announcement and talks about a new shipping lane. Ukraine is getting worse - three straight days of drone attacks and one strike that killed at least 37 people near Kyiv.
easy.markets: Oil got cheaper this week - Brent fell about 5% to roughly $88 a barrel - because traders think the strait is closer to reopening. But the price a ship pays to insure one trip is still several times what it was before the war, and that is the number that decides when tankers actually come back.
brief: The US announced the strait's shipping lanes are free of mines. But the shipping safety groups still call it dangerous and insurers have not cut their prices, so ships are mostly still staying away.

Iran and Oman agreed on a narrow temporary lane for ships that starts and ends inside Iran's own waters. That turns using the strait into something Iran gives permission for, instead of a right every country already has.

Russia hit Ukraine with drones for a third night in a row, and a strike near Kyiv killed at least 37 people. Russia attacks the power grid every year just before winter, and peace talks are frozen while it happens.

About 2,500 people are still missing after the flood on the Nepal-China border, and hundreds of them are foreign visitors. That pulls other governments in to help, and the flood also destroyed Nepal's main trade road to China.

risk.line: Two things moved in opposite directions since midday. On Hormuz the political track improved: CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Aug 27 that the internationally recognized transit routes are free of Iranian sea mines, following the President's own all-clear on Aug 26, and Iran and Oman confirmed a temporary joint navigation corridor plus a joint clearance project. The commercial track did not follow - the Joint Maritime Information Center holds its assessment at SEVERE with drifting or uncharted mines still flagged in and near the traffic separation scheme, UKMTO keeps mine-danger areas active, and war-risk cover reported at 7.5-10% of hull value is the actual gate. Brent near $87.58, off roughly 5.1% on the week, is the market splitting the difference. Against that, Ukraine got worse: 233 drones downed overnight into Aug 29 on a third day of near-continuous alerts, at least 37 killed in a strike near Kyiv, and Moscow's position still on the deep pause Peskov described Aug 28. Net assessment held at ELEVATED - the Gulf tail is being negotiated down while the war already running is being escalated on schedule.

forecasts.note: Transits rose 30% week-on-week to 114, and the same week JMIC counted single-digit vessels a day — both true, both about a tenth of the 130/day baseline. Mine clearance and insurance re-rating are physical clocks: Suez took roughly a year to clear after 1974
Brent 88.29, a fourth quiet mid-band session and -5% on the week. Band survival is realized vol times remaining time, and with 26 days left both terms improved; both tails weakened too

Two months on, Israel says the Lebanese army has fallen short on dismantling Hezbollah infrastructure. Fortna: ceasefires with an agreed verifier hold far better, and this one still has none while the party being disarmed rejects the premise

Kinetic down, jurisdiction up is the ratchet signature. Capped at +5; the stated tell is what the coast guard does through the Sept 24 visit.

Held to +7 because the Munir offer is a real concession, and $4.10 gas before midterms is real evidence against premeditation.

hypotheses.name: NEW · A pre-announcement leak into oil futures
hypotheses.d: Four times in the war window, nine- and ten-figure short bets landed 15–20 minutes before an Iran announcement: ~$2.2bn across crude, gasoil and gasoline before Trump's Mar 23 pause post; ~$950m before the Apr 7 ceasefire; ~$760m before Iran said Hormuz would open. ~$7bn total; CFTC probing, four members of Congress demanding answers. Split: deliberate leak 45 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 25 / coincidence 10. This is the only entry in the book whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event rather than pattern-matched after — which is why it opens this high. Against it: no episode has surfaced around this week's diplomacy.

hypotheses.d: Both its live predictions came in favourably this week and it gets credit for neither: the rival leverage hypothesis predicted the same things, and shared predictions are ambience. One more failed pre-summit call and it goes to the epitaph list.

brief.h: Washington declared the strait mine-free; the people who actually decide have not repriced it
brief.t: CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Aug 27 that internationally recognized transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz are free of Iranian sea mines, following the President's own all-clear on Aug 26. The bodies shipping actually obeys did not follow. The Joint Maritime Information Center still assesses the threat as SEVERE and warns of drifting or uncharted mines in and near the traffic separation scheme, and UKMTO keeps mine-danger areas active. Iran's deputy foreign minister answered that no one but Iran knows where the mines are and called the announcement market manipulation - that is a claim rather than a fact, but it is a claim underwriters have to price. Brent sat near $87.58, off about 5.1% on the week: the market read the declaration as real progress while the strait stayed commercially shut.
brief.context: The connective move is that a military all-clear and a commercial reopening are set by two different desks, and only one of them is in Washington. Reopening is priced by war-risk underwriting committees in London and by the protection-and-indemnity clubs - the mutual liability cover without which a tanker cannot call at most ports - that withdrew effective Mar 5. Their arithmetic is not political: premia went from roughly 1-3% of hull value before the February war to 7.5-10% by July per S&P Global, and on a laden VLCC worth about $300m in ship and cargo a single loss erases years of collected premium, so the rational underwriter demands protracted calm rather than a press release. Note the credit-claiming tell - US officials described the clearance work as contractor-led as recently as Aug 25, and this declaration credits the US military; when one operation acquires two authors in three days, somebody needs the win more than the work required. Base rate: insurance markets lag political all-clears by months, and verified clearance after both the 1974 Suez effort and the 1987-88 Gulf campaign ran on multi-month clocks with navies doing the lifting. Falsifier, dated and public: published war-risk rates falling back under 3% of hull value before Oct 31 would mean underwriters bought the declaration and the slow-clock argument is wrong.

brief.h: Iran and Oman have agreed a seven-mile corridor that begins and partly exits inside Iranian territorial waters
brief.t: Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi confirmed that Tehran and Muscat agreed a temporary joint navigation corridor through the strait, roughly 7 miles or 11.3km wide, entering through Iranian territorial waters with part of the exit route also inside them, alongside a joint mine-clearing project. Oman's foreign minister Badr Albusaidi carried it in Tehran with Araghchi, and both sides said the Gulf littoral states should be consulted so any arrangement respects neighbouring sovereignty. Tehran's stated condition is unchanged: full reopening waits on Washington honouring the June interim deal, which has since lapsed.
brief.context: This is the actual prize, and it was never about mines. Under the law of the sea a strait used for international navigation carries a right of transit passage the coastal state cannot suspend; a negotiated lane inside territorial waters converts that right into a permission - renewable, conditional, revocable by the state that grants it. That is the Sound Dues logic: Denmark grew rich for four centuries not by closing the Danish straits but by making passage something you were granted rather than owed, and it is why Iran does not need Hormuz shut, only conditional. Follow the money and the second-order loser is not the US Navy but Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, whose barrels would ride a lane negotiated over their heads by two governments and policed by one of them - which is exactly why the consult-the-littorals language is in the announcement, and why their answer is the thing to watch. The deciding desk is Iran's Supreme National Security Council with the IRGC Navy as operator, not the foreign ministry that reads it out. Falsifier: if tanker traffic normalizes through the internationally recognized traffic separation scheme rather than through the Iran-Oman corridor, the permit-regime read is wrong and this was only a bridging measure.

brief.h: Russia opened the winter grid campaign early, and the binding constraint is interceptor stock, not resolve
brief.t: Ukraine's air force said it shot down or suppressed 233 Russian drones overnight into Aug 29, a third consecutive day of near-continuous air alerts, after two straight days of strikes on the Kyiv region that hit more than a dozen apartment blocks and storage depots. A strike near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, among the deadliest of the year. Peskov said on Aug 28 that peace talks sit on a deep pause while Russian forces press their eastern offensive, with the demand for all of Donetsk unchanged.
brief.context: Constraint before character: this is not rage, it is a seasonal instrument running on a calendar. Russia has mounted a pre-heating-season campaign against Ukraine's grid every year since 2022 because electricity is the one target that converts military tempo into civilian political pressure on a schedule, and opening in late August rather than October buys extra weeks of degradation while repair crews still have daylight and roads. The rail underneath is a cost-exchange ratio, not willpower - a Shahed-type airframe costs a small fraction of the interceptor that kills it, so the variable that decides the winter is Ukrainian magazine depth and the European resupply pipeline, both of which have been described as depleted through August. That is also why the deep pause and the drone surge are one policy rather than two: you do not settle while your only compellent instrument is still ramping. The base rate is the honest part - three prior winters of grid campaigns produced blackouts and real suffering but no capitulation and no movement in Kyiv's negotiating position, so the prior on this one forcing terms is low. Falsifier: a Russian-confirmed talks round before Oct 15 would show the surge was a bargaining anchor rather than a seasonal campaign.

brief.h: The Tibet flood turned into a multi-government consular event, which is what actually mobilises resources
brief.t: Search work on the Nepal-China border is now running against roughly 2,500 people missing across both sides, with more than 1,300 still unaccounted for in the latest tallies and at least 700 of the missing being foreign nationals, dozens of them American. The Aug 26 glacial rock-and-ice failure on the Lhende destroyed the Gyirong Port complex, Nepal's principal land gateway to China, and the debris-dammed barrier lake breached on Aug 28.
brief.context: The number that changed the politics is the foreign one. A disaster in a low-income downstream state competes for attention and loses; one holding several hundred foreign nationals with Americans among them pulls in embassies, evacuation assets and cabinet-level phone calls within days, and that is the mechanism by which Kathmandu gets help it could not otherwise command. That is not cynicism, it is how disaster response is actually financed. The reason so many foreigners were in that valley is the same reason the corridor matters: Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong is both the trekking gateway and the trade route Nepal deliberately built up after the 2015 Indian blockade to cut its dependence on Indian transit, so a single valley failure takes out the tourism season and the diversification strategy together. The structural gap underneath is unchanged - no transboundary hydrological data-sharing on rivers that rise in Tibet and fall into Nepal, which is why Kathmandu is still asking questions about an event that began behind a closed border. Base rate: Himalayan glacial-lake and rock-ice failures are rising with warming and this catchment has essentially no automated upstream telemetry, so recurrence is not a tail event. What would change the read is an announced bilateral telemetry or data-sharing arrangement on the Lhende, not another aid pledge.

lesson: Today's most useful skill is not geopolitical, it is arithmetic, and it has a name: the rate-versus-level swap. This week USNI reported that Strait of Hormuz transits rose more than 30% week-on-week, 114 vessels against about 85. The same week, the Joint Maritime Information Center reported traffic still at reduced levels, with independent tracking showing single-digit vessels a day in both directions. Both are accurate and neither is spin - one reports a rate of change, the other a level - but a 30% gain off a collapsed base still leaves the strait at roughly a tenth of its pre-war 130 transits a day, and only one of those two sentences makes you feel the crisis is ending. The tell is simple and portable: when you are handed a percentage change, ask for the level and the denominator; when you are handed a level, ask for the trend. This is base-rate neglect from the analyst's bias checklist wearing a press-release costume, and a first cousin of the field guide's twelfth technique, the denied control - compared to what? One honesty note, because this wing of the canon teaches how minds are fooled and so must not itself cite fooled science: base-rate neglect and framing effects replicate robustly, while the social-priming results once bundled with them did not, and we do not lean on those.

lecture.title: The Economic Weapon: Why Sieges Make the Wars They Mean to Prevent

sections.t: Treasury designated roughly sixty Chinese “teapot” refiners — the small plants buying discounted Iranian crude — while touching no Chinese state major and no bank. The same week, central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the quarter gold fell over 20%. Two stories, one machine.

sections.h: Follow the money, name the mechanism
sections.t: A reserve manager buying into a 20% drawdown is not trading. He is hedging ACCESS — the risk that an asset held abroad gets switched off by its host government — and gold is the only large reserve asset with no counterparty who can flip that switch. Name the mechanism: the ECONOMIC WEAPON, using the financial plumbing whose hubs one country owns to inflict a siege without laying one. Iran discounts crude to Chinese teapots paying through dollar-touching chains; Treasury designates them; the IRGC's Strait Authority recoups the shortfall in Hormuz tolls. Sanction and gold bar are one transaction seen from two ends.

sections.h: Deep history I — the blockade that became an idea
sections.t: The economic weapon has a birthday and a founding failure. The birthday is November 1806, when Napoleon's Berlin Decrees declared the British Isles blockaded — the Continental System, an attempt to beat a maritime power by closing a continent's markets to it. It succeeded at nothing except generating enforcement. Portugal would not comply, so France invaded in 1807 and got the Peninsular War, the ulcer that bled the Grande Armée for six years. Alexander I quit the system in December 1810 because it was ruining Russian trade, and in 1812 Napoleon marched east to enforce it. The blockade never defeated Britain; it manufactured the two wars that destroyed the blockader. Sanctions require enforcement, and enforcement against a determined leakage path tends toward conquest. The second case mattered because it worked. The Allied blockade of Germany ran from 1914 through the armistice and was lifted only when Germany signed at Versailles in June 1919. German official estimates put civilian deaths from malnutrition near 424,000 — contested, and historians still argue how much was blockade and how much German agricultural mismanagement. But perception makes policy, and a generation concluded hunger had beaten an undefeated army. So they institutionalized it as a PEACE instrument: Article 16 of the League Covenant made sanctions automatic against an aggressor, and Wilson in 1919 put it in words no Treasury official would dare use today — “A nation that is boycotted is a nation that is in sight of surrender. Apply this economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy and there will be no need for force.” The weapon was invented to ABOLISH war; the rest of the century refutes that sentence.

sections.h: Deep history II — the failures that define our problem
sections.t: ABYSSINIA, 1935. Italy invaded Ethiopia; the League invoked Article 16 — exempting oil, coal and steel, and never closing the Suez Canal, which Britain controlled and through which Italian troopships sailed. Mussolini won anyway. The sanctions were real enough to enrage and too porous to stop, and the lesson is sharper than “sanctions don't work”: a sanction calibrated to spare the sender teaches the target that the sender is deterred too. Then the second-order effect. Nicholas Mulder's argument in The Economic Weapon is that the interwar regime deterred small states and PROVOKED large ones. Italy, Germany and Japan drew the same conclusion from the 1930s — dependence on seaborne trade was a vulnerability an enemy could switch off at will, and the answer was autarky, self-sufficiency taken by force. Lebensraum and the Co-Prosperity Sphere were ideological projects; they were also sanctions-proofing programs. Japan is the proof case. Washington embargoed scrap iron in 1940, then froze Japanese assets on 26 July 1941; America supplied roughly 80% of Japan's oil, and with Britain and the Dutch East Indies following, Japan lost about 88% of its oil imports. Reserves would last three years at peace, half that at war — Nagano's image was of a patient wasting away, every month of compliance leaving Japan weaker against the enemy it expected to fight. Pearl Harbor came in December. And the detail that turns story into discipline: the freeze was never meant to be total. Roosevelt intended a licensing regime keeping oil flowing so the tap stayed usable as leverage; officials in State and Treasury administered it so strictly that no licences issued and the flow stopped. The sanction that helped produce Pearl Harbor was substantially an organizational outcome, not a presidential decision — Allison's Essence of Decision, live. Before inferring “Iran's strategy” from one action, ask which bureau took it.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: The leakage path is always the whole story — not the designation list, the leak: Portugal and Russia in 1806, Beira and Pretoria in 1966, Chinese teapots now. NOW THE BREAK. Japan in 1941 had a military option that promised to SOLVE its resource problem: seize the Dutch East Indies and own the oil. Iran has none — it fought its war, lost the conventional exchange, and has played its asymmetric card, the Hormuz toll. Nor did 1914 face an alternative supplier: Iran's is the world's second-largest economy, which the sanctioner just spared. Less Pearl Harbor, more Rhodesia.

MULDER says the siege provokes: strangulation drives large states to autarky, then preemption. DREZNER says sanctions are cheap theater — Hufbauer's data give a third success rate at best, near zero against great powers. The 2026 evidence buries neither: it splits by SIDE, and the split is the finding. On the TARGET Mulder scores: gold, stockpiles, payment rails, enrichment acceleration under maximum pressure. On the SENDER Drezner scores harder — the carve-outs. Sixty teapots and not one bank is not escalation; it is the sanctioner taking its own threat hostage, because hitting a Chinese bank endangers the dollar system that makes the hammer heavy.

The 2015 architecture is not coming back (high confidence): the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves turned the settlement network into an instrument; a hedge once bought is not resold. Expect bifurcation, not de-dollarization (moderate-high). EICHENGREEN is right that currencies erode glacially; the WEAPON depreciates faster than the CURRENCY. The bolder call (moderate): the most dangerous decade is the one in which the weapon still works but no longer terrifies. Mulder's mechanism fires in the transition — invested in escaping, not finished, expecting strangulation regardless. For China, the 2030s — so Economic D-Day may SHORTEN the fuse it was meant to lengthen. FALSIFIER: designate a major Chinese state bank; if Beijing cuts Iranian purchases within a quarter, I am wrong. Two centuries say the economic weapon does not replace war — it sorts the world into blocs that survive each other's sieges, then gives the survivors a reason to fight.

Nicholas Mulder, The Economic Weapon (2022) — published weeks before the Russia sanctions matched its template. Farrell & Newman, “Weaponized Interdependence” (2019) — it called the 2022 playbook and the chip controls in advance. Eichengreen, Exorbitant Privilege — the counterweight.

fired: None today. Every named wire was checked against its threshold and none met it - logged deliberately so the non-fire is scoreable.

No new attack at the strait since the Kuwaiti tanker Al Salam II was holed above the waterline on Aug 26, already logged on the 27th. Nothing met the stricter wording either: a US-flagged or US-escorted vessel, or an attack Iran publicly claims.

Near-wire, not fired: the record 244 Chinese government ships around Taiwan is the same gray-zone ratchet the Taiwan wire watches, but that wire's threshold is mobilization-type activity and survey hulls are not it. Not counting it is the discipline; saying so is the record.
